newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Banks set up team to settle sugar miller bad loan.
newsitem.headline: Banks set up team to settle sugar miller bad loan.

text.p: Philippine sugar millers and planters on Friday pleaded with government officials for protection after the country's biggest miller reported a debt problem and bankers set up committee to negotiate rescheduling.

The sugar industry representatives meeting with government officials at the Malacanang presidential palace ended without any solutions to the problems of Victorias Milling Company, which on Thursday secured a moratorium for 90 days on debts amounting to 4.423 billion pesos ($168 million).
"That's the one we wanted to avoid," Executive Secretary Ruben Torres told Reuters.
Other officials said the meeting discussed an earlier plea to raise tariffs on imported sugar, a proposal that has gained strength after Victorias financial troubles emerged.
The 32 banks which lent money to Victorias, the country's largest miller, on Friday set up a committee to negotiate with the company.
"The representatives of the creditors will in effect study and coordinate with the management of the company." the head of the committee, Jose Pastor Puno, told Reuters.
Puno, who is first vice president of PCIBank which is one of the creditors, said the committee would meet on Monday to consider the various alternatives.
An official of Philippine National Bank, who said the bank made short-term loans of 349,764 pesos to Victorias, said: "I think we will see a long-term restructuring of the account."

Of the total outstanding loans of 4.423 billion pesos, 2.778 billion are short-term loans and analysts said these could cause problems as the company would not be in a position to repay them at maturity.

An official of Land Bank of the Philippines, who confirmed loans of over 500 million pesos to Victorias, said the assets covered by the mortgage trust deed would be reappraised and that the expected value was enough to cover the creditors' exposure.

A list of creditors given to Reuters by one of the banks showed that among foreign banks with varying exposure to Victorias were Citibank, ANZ Bank, Deutsche Bank, Hong Kong Shanghai Bank and Banco National de Paris
On Friday, Victorias denied reports its troubles were caused by an overly ambitious expansion plan funded by debt.
"The financial difficulties of VMC is not solely attributable to the 'financing most of its expansion programme through debt', but the present state of the sugar industry," it said in a statement.

The company's income statement showed short-term bank loans in 1996 rose sharply to 4.496 billion pesos in 1996 from 2.930 billion in 1995. Long-term debt rose to 2.379 billion pesos from 1.854 billion. The company reported a net loss of 242 million pesos against a profit of 105 million in 1995. "To ease its outrageously high debt levels, VMC is selling several idle assets to raise cash," brokerage Philippine Asia Equity said in a December report when it recommended a speculative buy on the stock.
On Friday, Victorias stock dropped like a stone, falling 1.30 pesos, or 28.89 percent, to 3.20 pesos.
Shares of some of the creditor banks also fell in early trade but later recovered as investors realised the loans were a small part of the banks' overall loan portfolios.
Philippine sugar companies have been plagued by a sugar glut since last year after the country imported large quantities.
Local sugar prices have fallen to 500 pesos a 50 kg bag from 800 to 900 at the beginning of 1996.
